comments.body:
The Wall Street Journal is certainly entitled to take a position on the WNBA and its policies. But the tone of the editorial “Boys Will Be Boys” was remarkably dismissive of the women who have worked their entire lives to compete at the highest level of professional basketball.

The line, “Yet until the WNBA does, Messrs. Kanter and White are having some fun,” is particularly troubling. Whatever one’s position on the underlying issue, describing two former NBA players as “having some fun” at the expense of a women’s professional sports league reduces a legitimate and complicated discussion to a joke, with the women themselves serving as the punchline.

The editorial board could have made its argument thoughtfully and seriously. Instead, phrases like “Boys Will Be Boys” and “having some fun” come across as smug and belittling toward female professional athletes who have fought for decades for their sport to be taken seriously.

There is room for vigorous debate about eligibility, sex, gender, and fairness in women’s sports. Those issues deserve serious discussion. But women athletes also deserve the basic respect of not having their careers and their league used as entertainment for men trying to make a political point.

I expect better judgment—and frankly, better journalism—from the editorial board of The Wall Street Journal.

Freedom may be part of happiness, but it also includes, for most of us I believe, having enough of the basics so that we can breathe easily and enjoy friends, family, the outdoors and more. Happiness surely is diminished with food scarcity, lack of adequate housing, poor access to health care, and more. 
I believe in caring communities , and it is the role of government to help us create them. 
Capitalism can be part of this, as long as the "pursuit of wealth" does not overtake all other valuable goals. 
How much do we need?  How many bathrooms, giant cars the size of some living rooms, do we need to feel happy?
Most of us know, I think, that true happiness lies in loving relationships and having enough.

Some folks on this thread ask  -- quite reasonably -- of what use is reading a 1000-page book?  My vague answer might be the "big-picture brain" that can ask questions and pose scenarios outside the parameters of the initial question one encounters.  I've seen this in the best consultants -- and educators -- I've met.  Even seen a lawyer or two get dragged to that level, though with some reluctance.

 Dostoevsky is good stuff read to in late adolescence, as personal philosophies take shape, though still with a plasticity that allows for dialogue and questioning.  And more of a page-turner -- no, really! -- than your average philosophy tome.

Your article has brought back fond memories of my favorite high school English teacher, whose passion for Melodrama theater imbued his teaching on a daily basis.  I found his style very engaging; it helped me persist through the occasional assignment I found tiresome.

I always counseled the  student teachers  I was sent to mentor that to be successful in classroom you needed to "love" and be excited about the subject you were teaching so that your students would be excited as you; to be knowledgeable of the subject -- in depth and breadth  -- as possible; to encourage the students to challenge  your knowledge  of the subject ( on a personal level,  I told my students  if they thought a point I made was  an error they were to let me know and I would allow them to go to the library -- I taught before the widespread use of computers in the classroom -- and told them if their research verified what I said, all well and good.  BUT if they found I was in error we BOTH were wiser for the experience.)
Teaching is a cooperative activity that educates both the student and the teacher.

That said, I harbor a bit of skepticism about the mechanics of this victory. Furthermore, it doesn't strike me as a particularly "eccentric" pedagogical strategy at all. Ultimately, it’s a highly enjoyable essay from a professor who has managed, quite beautifully, to convince himself that he pulled off a masterstroke.

comments.name: Barry B

comments.name: Anthony Alfero

Even when SCOTUS has settled a debate, hack lefty judges ignore these rulings and rule based on the agenda of the hard left.

comments.name: Jim C

In Trump v. U.S. in 2024 the Trump "originalist" majority asserts that the founders intended that presidents should be allowed to trade pardons for millions, pressure state election officials to commit fraud, brow beat his IRS into being prohibited from auditing him, his family and businesses all of which Trump has done in reliance on SCOTUS's Trump v. U.S.  R.I.P. formerly respectable "originalism."

comments.name: Richard L

comments.name: Peter G Wales
comments.body: The body of law being promulgated by the courts since 2016 (Trump), needs to be added to the civics curriculum across the land. (Dobbs, Kennedy, Humphrey's Executor, et al) It applies "fixed meaning" legal science the way it was understood publicly when enacted , (aka originalism), following the Christopher Columbus Langdell IRAC methodology, he taught at Harvard to insure rule of law and Scalia, demonstrated on the SCOTUS. It restrains the court, denies judicial activism as unconstitutional and restores the American rule of law. School Boards need to be held accountable.

comments.name: Paul Boocock
comments.body: I think so. If Hunter and Blyleven and Sutton and Morris and Kaat are in, he should be in. I'm for a more inclusive hall. Not because I want the standards lowered, but because there are already players like the ones I just listed who ARE in the Hall. There are lesser players in the Hall. DP combo Tinker to Evers to Chance are in just because they sounded poetic! There were better DP combos even in those times. Tommy John was an actual ace pitcher for almost 10 years, the guy you wanted on the mound for the big games; and then he was a viable #3 starter for another 10 years. I don't think you should hold the #3 starter years against him.

comments.name: Dan Hewson
comments.body: Of course Tommy  John belongs in the Hall of Fame. I would  think it likely that there are some pitchers with lesser numbers in the Hall, and if not, create a special category relating to his surgery and longevity.

comments.name: J.A.R.
comments.body: I certainly think that given his overall pitching numbers coupled with the very first implementation of an experimental surgery that has had a major impact on the sport of baseball, Mr John should be inducted to the HOF. How about the very next vote?

comments.name: The Old Ranger
comments.body: He was tricky. You hated to see him on the mound against your team when he was in his prime. As for the Hall, my guess is the writers could not see past the surgery. The big surprise is that the assorted veterans committees overlooked him. Obviously he wasn’t part of the in crowd.

comments.name: West Side Dame
comments.body: What an amazing story! Thanks for telling it. I agree that a player with that much talent and tenacity should, indeed, belong in the Baseball Hall of Fame.

comments.name: just saying~

comments.name: Gus Fring

comments.name: MJ

articles.summary: After tearing an elbow ligament, he underwent a risky procedure and returned at his best, changing baseball and giving new hope to injured players.

comments.name: Northeast kitchen
comments.body: I arranged for a charge account at a local bookstore for each of my 4 great-grandchildren. Each account is good for 2 books  a month for a year. The kids must choose the books themselves. So far it has been fun and interesting. It's a pretty good way to get children interested in books and in building their own expanding interests.

comments.name: Alexis Ludwig
comments.body: Love this piece.  Puts reading onto an informed historical and absolutely current perspective, pushing back against facile gloom and doom with realistic reasons for optimism.  We need more of this, and reading in whatever useful form it can take.  Knowing and learning from what other thinking people have thought, including those who lived long ago or live far away, seems like the kind of thing human beings should continue doing, if we're smart.

comments.name: GM
comments.body: Speaking as a veteran teacher of the Philadelphia inner city schools, literacy is going to remain a problem. Even people with degrees are often able to read words but digest little. There are few national papers written above a 6th grade level and often remain with 5th. Until students are motivated to attend class, teachers have academic freedom, unions and administrators aren't the driving forces, stagnation is the result. Private schooled students will have a future along with a few public schools in suburbia.

comments.name: LesBom
comments.body:
ReadAloud West Virginia puts about 1000 volunteers into classrooms across the state primarily in K - 5.  The object is to motivate kids to read for fun.  Readers are oriented and respond to teachers requesting readers.  
After 10 years, my mantra is "Never underestimate the kids."  Our reading is never test material; we do book distributions so kids can own books and mostly they get to choose the books.
The intent is to create readers who would be drawn to Mr Schmidt's events and libraries.
Much more to say here: "I could write a book about it."

comments.name: Eleanor
comments.body:
I honestly don't understand why anyone would need to gather with a group for 'silent reading.' Or sign up for a weekend getaway to read. 

But I'm glad that bookstores are becoming gathering places. Long may it last.

comments.name: Fritzmillian
comments.body:
Hi, my name's Cole. (Chorus: Hi: Hi Cole) I'm a 75 year old academic suffering from bibliophilia disorder. As I try to downsize, each beloved tome I select to give to the library booksale cuts me to the quick. I have tried to make a pledge with my sponsor (wife of 40 years) that I will give one to the library for each new one I acquire. But I'm too weak. She is also co-dependent on our library.
I am glad to see folks concerned about poor reading skills and habits of younger people, but I must quibble with the author's premise that young people want information about the world they inhabitat, not the world of the internet. If that were true, aspiring to be a tik tok influencer would not be a thing.

comments.name: Jean
comments.body:
The headline is misleading.

The story is actually about how book clubs continue to evolve AS TOOLS FOR COMPANIONSHIP,

comments.name: Mountain girl
comments.body: As an English teacher at a special act school in New York State - my students were neurodivergent and adjudicated. I utilized theatre and texts of many different plays to explore literature -including Oscar Wilde, George Bernard Shaw , August Wilson, Carson McCullers and many other playwrights. We explored not only the American experience but European art and history through drama. I had astounding success and students who had difficulty reading, directed and coached the class readings. We probably had to much fun for the administration’s liking but it was a great way to teach literature and encourage literacy with no pain

articles.title: This Is the Solution to America’s Literacy Crisis, and It’s a Lot of Fun
articles.summary: Come join the fun.

comments.name: Joel M
comments.body: The purpose of all AI ventures is to make money for their investors. Social benefit isn't part of the equation. What developers like me are learning is the limitation of AI coding. for writing corporate speak it's great, for coming up with new ideas it's imitative. However it seems to be great at replacing the traditional skill of thinking with automation

comments.name: David Greene
comments.body: Interesting but perhaps incomplete. There is an underlying idea in this that writing is only done in English or Literature classes. The study of any social science or history requires all of the skills mentioned. In high schools in class writing as in the essay portion in class tests is still quite common, and AI can be taught to use as another research aid for out of class assignments.

comments.name: Howard Herman
comments.body: This article is very timely and directly on point. When students start relying heavily on technology they lose some of their ability for independent and creative thought. This reminds me of when calculators became readily available and people stopped doing some math matters in their heads. To this day I see time and again in stores and restaurants when cash is used to pay a bill how difficult it is for many workers to figure out the correct change due. Technology is truly a great thing, it has improved our lives in many ways. But don’t forget basic life skills that still provide a good foundation for moving forward and working with technology.

comments.name: justgimmesometruth
comments.body:
I'm nearing 80. In 7th grade, every Friday was essay day in English class. The entire class time was spent writing an essay that was graded for ideas, organization, spelling, and everything else that matters. The subjects were generally interesting, and I remember looking forward to expressing myself in this way (just as I enjoy writing these comments). And the teacher put a lot of work into grading those essays.

No written work should be graded unless it is produced in class and supervised. Fine to practice writing with homework assignments, but grades for writing need to be based on work done in class with paper and pen.

The decline in the quality of student writing started well before the rise of AI. AI has now done us a favor. It will force all teachers back to basing grades on work done in class under supervision. 

And this may be an unpopular opinion, but I believe that the crop of teachers working in the NYC schools in the post-war decades, were unusually skilled and dedicated. In later decades, many of these people would take jobs in the computer field or engineering, but back then, they became teachers.

My aunt, who worked in a school office, never called these people 'teachers', she always called them 'educators'. And she said it with the same sense of awe as when she pronounced the word 'doctor'.

comments.name: pbcal
comments.body: Please don't ignore the fact that AI is partisan.  If students can't differentiate between neutrality, their own ideas of social justice or those of the opposing parties, we are losing thinkers and fighters.

comments.name: Margaret H Koonce
comments.body: Great literature and poetry written by humans, in all their complexity, has shined a light in the darkness for many an individual. Great writing can change lives.  Come to that, save lives.  What grief I feel if we lose these gifts and capacities to write and read.  And to dig ditches.

comments.name: Dandelion
comments.body:
By the time they reach college, most students will be familiar with chatbots. Unless they've lived without access to computers, they'll have used AI all day long. They don't need further instruction in how to do so. 
What fewer and fewer of them know is how to use their own brains to analyse anything, or to produce written work. Nor do most of them even realize what they're losing by relying so much on AI.

comments.name: Kathy
comments.body:
I understand that some feel using AI to be less than beneficial for learning and writing.  I disagree.  I do the reading assigned as a college student. I explain my rough response to AI and it comes out with something less than I want. We go back and forth until after the fifth or sixth revision,  the work is done. Could I do this alone? Yes. After many hours. But. As a mom of five, a 24/7 caregiver for my husband with dementia,   and all the tasks of keeping a household running smoothly,  there is no "many hours". 
I do not know the answer to this challenge.  I do believe each of us is on our own journey and we each use what we need to get through this life. And there is no shame in using available tools.

articles.title: What Do Students Lose When They Stop Writing?
articles.summary: Educators are worried that many students can no longer write essays without A.I. And it’s costing more than just grammar skills.

While I would prefer the crude and vulgar comments weren’t in the public sphere, it’s more important that we don’t give these people positions of power because we didn’t want to offend anyone by repeating these comments.

comments.body: It always amazes me how Americans seem to be so afraid of the word socialism and confuse it with communism. In Europe socialism is mainstream. And I don’t think we are doing too badly. comments.body:
I think silicon valley will discover, as the traditional defense contractors have discovered that the defense department is a "terrible" customer. Made worse by congressional dysfunction.

 The best way to secure profits is to capture "permanent" funding through artificial scarcity and high technology, high barrier to entry, equipment. After the military commits to a system, its a stable money supply for decades.

comments.name: Jomo
comments.body: What I'm curious about is how a teenager (Mr. Luckey, aptly named) could successfully found a company producing virtual reality headsets, a task that Silicon Valley titans were struggling with. He somehow figured out, as a kid, how to make the VR technology work including video screen, processor chip and power supply, and how to get all the components designed and manufactured, with a factory in China. At an age when the rest of us had just finished high school, when he's only barely old enough to sign a legal contract. How did he do it?

comments.name: SSColorado
comments.body:
I'm regularly amazed at how viciously self-proclaimed free market capitalists rail against socialism but utterly fail to recognize how much our biggest and most profitable businesses began with government funding and/or with the government as the first market. 

From tech and the Internet DoD funding and buying to pharmaceuticals research funded by the government to our transportation system (railroads, interstate highways, and aviation) to agriculture supported with infrastructure projects like dams and rural electrification, what made America what it is today was actually socialist projects.

comments.body: So trends show commoditization of AI (via locally run open-weight models). comments.body: This Trump Derangement Syndrome is all-encompassing in the media. Do you think maybe just maybe a voter will vote for the best candidate going forward?

comments.body: Getting abortions banned only buys you so much good will.  It's also clear that Trump never cared about that and he always did it to cater to the evangelicals.  After that, like most politicians his taken his core of support for granted.  Perhaps those folks are finally wising up.  It's not only the economic damage, but also the corruption, and destruction of the rule of law that has always made America great.

comments.body: I'll believe it when I see it, but it would be great if farmers finally figured out just who has been boning them.....

comments.name: Andrew Connors

The most glaring omission from this article is the fact that many Iowans believe nominee Lahn is a Kansan and not an Iowan.  

Until he clearly and definitively explains whether he plans to spend the majority of his time in Des Moines or Wichita, Sand will continue to lead.

comments.name: Charlie Roast
comments.body: Lahn, inviting the dangerous quack to join him on the campaign trail, is a big mistake. Jr. is not popular in Iowa.

comments.name: Evan B
comments.body: People want to be better off financially. Raising taxes will never help, even if it's on other countries. Starting yet another "woah woah, wait, why are we doing this" war also won't ever help. It's not hard to see why politicians have bad reputations: they lie, they don't know what they're doing, and they're spineless.

comments.name: Alberto
comments.body: I have family in Cuba. We sent them a generator. It took forty days to arrive in their small rural town, not far from Guatánamo. It was such a relief to learn that it had not been stolen or confiscated. They charge it during the two or three hours they get power. Power comes once a day, and sometimes every two or three days. The generator provides power for another three or four hours. We are still trying to find solar panels for them. You have to buy them through trusted intermediaries, like the one that delivered the generator. Otherwise, they will never get there.

comments.name: Craig Curie
comments.body: Hands off. All we are doing is adding to the suffering of regular people... as we do wherever we stick our noses. If we locked up all the world leaders -- and replaced them with intelligent 10-year-olds, I think they'd do a better job. Makes you wonder if the lust for power that propels a person to leadership... makes them into malevolent leaders.

comments.name: Guy V
comments.body:
The Cuban government bears enormous responsibility for decades of repression and economic mismanagement. But that does not justify a U.S. policy that deliberately makes ordinary Cubans more desperate in the hope that hardship will produce regime change.

Obama recognized that after more than fifty years, isolation had failed. His opening sought to expand trade, travel and contact with Cubans without endorsing their government. Trump has reversed that approach and gone much further by trying to choke off Cuba's fuel supplies through pressure on third countries. UN human-rights experts have called those measures a “serious violation of international law.”

Fuel deprivation means less electricity, transportation, refrigeration, food production and functioning health care. Ordinary Cubans inevitably pay the price.

We should press Havana on political prisoners, human rights and democratic reform. But after six decades, we should know better than to believe that making Cubans poorer and hungrier will make them freer. Shame on viceroy Rubio!

comments.name: Pancho
comments.body: Speaking of Venezula, there is still a big question of where the oil money is going. Very little has been sent to Venezula. There are billions unaccounted for and the administration as usual is stonewalling.

comments.name: Carlos in NH
comments.body: It is unlikely that the Trump administration would allow full democracy to be established in Cuba through free elections. What if a leftie were elected? This is also true of Venezuela. Also, Just consider Chile, Iran, Gaza, and elsewhere where voters elected a government that was unacceptable to the US. The net result has been either a US-sponsored coup d'etat or deadly sanctions that punish ordinary people.

comments.name: AM
comments.body: When Cuba embarked on its 1961 literacy campaign, CIA backed insurgents murdered student teachers and their campesino pupils. Castro declared war on these Batistiano insurgents and won. He arrived at the understandable conclusion that the U.S. would never allow Cuba to govern itself without interference and he consolidated power. Americans misunderstand how heavily this early era of post revolutionary history weighs on Cuba’s psyche. The Miami hardliners who dictate American policy are largely the descendants of these Batistianos. There is no love lost between them and Cubans from the island. By and large they blame the American economic embargo and oil blockade for their suffering, as they should. Of course the Cuban government has made mistakes, but it is inaccurate to compare them in any way to the 60+ year acts of war that the U.S. has perpetrated against Cuba.

comments.name: Keln

comments.name: Uncle Pennybags
comments.body: Macklemore was right about America

comments.body: For the past few weeks I’ve started to notice speed boats in the harbor.  I don’t know if these are supposed to be thrill rides because high-speed spins seem to be a major feature of these outings.

comments.name: DMO
comments.body: This problem emanate from New Jersey. It’s time to extend congestion pricing to the waterways.

comments.name: Jane
comments.body: The More You Know the Better It Goes: I am taking Coast Guard Auxiliary classes in Boothbay Harbor, Maine.  Amazing to learn so much. The local marine store had to order the chart that they wanted us to use in class, (along with the tools to do everything by hand), because the government is not printing the charts as, "Everyone has a Garmin!"  The marine store owner was thrilled and complemented me, " I think it's great that you are learning these things."  The compliment is to the Coast Guard Auxiliary.  There are only 3 of us in the class, and there are 4 fellows of the Coast Guard there helping us.  10 hours of classes for 40$ plus materials.  And private make up zoom classes when you miss.  I have one at 9am tomorrow.

comments.name: David Polakoff
comments.body:
I am so grateful for the work of the United States Coast Guard and the marine units of the NYPD, FDNY, United States Park Police, the State of New Jersey, and the New Jersey municipalities along the Gold Coast. Their resources are limited, however, and they cannot be everywhere all the time. It is understandable that their priorities are emergency response and counterterrorism.

But that leaves a vacuum when it comes to proactive enforcement against the “credit card captains” and the rogue behavior of jet ski operators. In a perfect world, federal, state, and city authorities and politicians would underwrite a fund for even basic, periodic patrols of the “Wild West” of the Hudson River below the George Washington Bridge, the East River, and the Upper New York Harbor.

Wyatt Earp of marine law enforcement, where art thou?

comments.name: Captain Dan
comments.body: Getting back to this preventable accident:  14 people on a 22 foot boat is clearly unsafe and every boater who saw this should have called the police.  Every boat manufacturer has a maximum passenger rating and for this boat it is probably 7 people maximum.  And this tragedy was a charter which classifies this as an Unsuspected Passenger Vessel which by law requires a USCG licensed Captain, commercial insurance and 6 passengers maximum.

comments.name: Deb
comments.body: The newest (coming) disaster: the Jet Skis coming into the river from New Jersey, zooming across all the channels toward Brooklyn Bridge Park, weaving in and out, racing one another without concern for the sailing school in our little marina where people are newly learning to handle a sailboat.  These are the same class of idiots who weave in and out of traffic at 80 mph on the Henry Hudson and the Sawmill Parkways, and the same kind of jerks who take over major roadways on motorcycles, mopeds and ATVs without any regard to pedestrians or other drivers.  I feel for the cops who have to protect us, and protect these jerks as well.  As far as the Jet Skis - shut down the owner/operators who rent them without offering classes in boating rules of the road.

comments.name: Patricia
comments.body: Several years ago, my husband and I bought tickets and took an evening sail on a big sailboat in the harbor. There were perhaps a dozen customers. There was no seating, we sat right on the deck of the sailboat. We weren’t given life jackets or a safety talk. I was sitting with my husband on the deck in an area where there was a chrome metal railing just a few inches high. It was windy and the boat moved quickly, and leaned quite severely. The angle felt very precarious and I could feel myself sliding. My husband struggled to hold on to me. I recall vividly looking at the churning water a couple of feet below and the little chrome rail and feeling sure I was going in.  I was frozen and couldn’t make a sound, just thought I should kick my shoes off so I can swim. After several minutes the boat righted itself and we turned back to the dock. I could hardly walk when we disembarked I was so shaken. Even now I sweat remembering.   We said nothing just shook our heads at how close we came to danger. Our own damn fault.

comments.name: Louis Santoro
comments.body: See, the Dodgers can be stopped!

comments.name: MARK GIBBONS
comments.body: Why doesn't he just get a pre-pardon?

comments.name: Mark Verhyden
comments.body: Looks like he skews a good bit to the left so this is no surprise.

comments.name: Larry Rybka
comments.body:
These aren't public companies, so the normal securities disclosure regime doesn't even apply to them directly. Yet the SEC still caught a reported $20 billion in undisclosed affiliated-party loans that the Delaware Department of Insurance - the regulator with actual jurisdiction over these insurers - apparently missed for years.

Two Dodd-Frank provisions set the table for exactly this kind of structure. The 2010 Harkin Amendment blocked the SEC's Rule 151A and kept indexed annuities under state-only oversight, by design. And Dodd-Frank's reinsurance credit reform handed sole authority over reinsurance collateral requirements to a single state - the ceding insurer's domicile - which is exactly the dynamic that let captive-friendly states compete toward lighter collateral rules. That's what made the offshore/onshore captive reinsurance trick so attractive to PE-owned insurers in the first place: cede reserves to an affiliate, post minimal real collateral, and call it capital.

Fifty-one state regulators, no consolidated view of an insurer group's related-party lending, and it took an agency with a completely different mandate to notice a multibillion-dollar concealment that Delaware had every tool to catch and didn't.

Walter hasn't been charged with anything. But the system that was supposed to catch this before it reached $20 billion was built with the cracks already in it.

It is misleading to compare missile defense or "star wars" as envisioned by Reagan with Patriot missiles and iron dome. The former imagines defending against potentially tens of thousands of intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBM's) while the latter is far more limited and only pertains to missiles that do not leave the atmosphere. 
Despite countless billions of taxpayer dollars being spent, we have never even come close to a system that would defend against ICBM's.
Ultimately, US national security would have been far better served had Reagan taken the deal rather than imaging that there was a technical solution to this human problem.

On a personal note: I went door to door with a TV crew in Baltimore while the summit was underway asking people how they felt about the Reagan/Gorbachev meeting. Overwhelmingly, normal American citizens expressed that their greatest hope was that the two leaders would reduce the threat of global annihilation. As it stands, they made progress but each and every day we still remain less than 30 minutes from total destruction.

The linguistic intelligentsia know that ‘intelligentsia’ is NOT the word ‘intelligent’ with the Greek suffix ‘-sia’ at the end. 

In English, ‘-sia’ usually appears in Greek-derived medical or psychological conditions, like amnesia, anesthesia, or dyslexia (where -ia means ‘condition’).

English borrowed the entire word intelligentsia directly from the 19th-century Russian word ‘intelligentsiya’.

Russian took the Latin noun intelligentia (intelligence) and added the Slavic suffix ‘-ya’ which functions like the English -ship (as in citizenship) or -dom (as in kingdom) transforming  the abstract concept of ‘being smart’ into a concrete group: a body of educated people.
